---
title: "How to Write Better AI Prompts: 5 Steps With Copy-Paste Examples"
subtitle: "A beginner's walkthrough with real prompts you can paste into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini today"
category: "how-to"
audience: "both"
read_time_minutes: 7
tags: ["prompting", "chatgpt", "claude", "gemini", "productivity", "getting-started"]
---

> **In short:** Better prompts come down to five habits: name a role, give examples, specify the format, paste your raw material, and iterate in the same chat. This guide walks through each habit as a numbered step, with a real prompt you can copy and paste.

## What you need before you start

This walkthrough works in any major AI chat tool: **ChatGPT**, **Claude**, or **Gemini**. No paid plan is required — the free versions handle every example below. You'll just need:

- A free account on whichever tool you prefer (sign-up takes about two minutes)
- A web browser on a phone or laptop
- About 10 minutes for your first prompt

Pick one task you actually need help with this week — a work email, a social caption, a meeting recap — so you can practice on something real.

## Step 1 — Name a role and an audience

Open your AI chat and start the conversation by telling the AI **who it should act as** and **who the answer is for**. Without this, the AI guesses a generic tone and a generic reader, and you get a generic answer.

In the message box, type the role and the reader in one sentence. You'll see the AI respond in a more focused voice right away.

💬 Copy-paste starter:
*You are a friendly social media manager writing for busy parents in their 30s.*

**You'll know it worked when** the AI's first reply feels aimed at a specific person, not at "everyone in general."

## Step 2 — Give the AI an example to match

If you have a piece of writing you already like — an email, a caption, a paragraph — paste it in and ask the AI to match the style. The AI pays close attention to length, rhythm, and word choice when it has a model to copy.

Find one short example (two or three sentences is plenty) and paste it into the chat before your actual request. Then write *"write something new in the same style about [your topic]."*

💬 Copy-paste starter:
*Here's a caption I like: "[paste your example]". Write three new captions in the same style for my coffee shop's weekend pastry menu.*

**You'll know it worked when** the new output sounds like it could sit next to your example without anyone noticing the switch.

## Step 3 — Specify the format and length

Don't leave the shape of the answer up to chance. A clear instruction at the end of your prompt — like *"bulleted list,"* *"under 100 words,"* or *"three options"* — makes the AI far more likely to deliver something usable on the first try.

Add one line at the end of your prompt describing the format. The AI will usually follow it without further nudging.

💬 Copy-paste starter:
*Give me three gift ideas for a friend who loves hiking, under $50 each. Return them as a bulleted list with one sentence of reasoning each.*

**You'll know it worked when** the response matches the shape you asked for — three bullets, each short, each with a reason — instead of a single block of paragraphs.

## Step 4 — Paste your raw material into the prompt

The biggest upgrade most people miss: **give the AI the actual stuff to work with.** A job ad, a meeting transcript, your rough notes, a recipe you want to adapt. The more real material you paste in, the more personal the answer gets.

Before you hit send, look at your prompt and ask: *"Is there a document, link summary, or paragraph I could paste that would make this less generic?"* If yes, paste it above your instruction.

💬 Copy-paste starter:
*Here's the job ad: "[paste ad]. Here's my experience: [paste 3–4 bullet points]. Write a 150-word cover letter that matches the ad's tone.*

**You'll know it worked when** the cover letter mentions specifics from the job ad and from your experience — not vague phrases like "I'm a hard worker."

## Step 5 — Iterate in the same chat

If the first answer isn't right, **don't start a new chat.** Reply in the same conversation with a small, specific change. The AI remembers everything above, so each follow-up sharpens the previous attempt.

Type one short instruction at a time: *"make it more friendly,"* *"cut it in half,"* *"add a question at the end."* Watch how the response shifts.

💬 Copy-paste follow-up:
*Good start — make it sound less formal and end with a friendly question to the reader.*

**You'll know it worked when** the new version clearly reflects your tweak, and you only needed one or two rounds to get something you'd actually send.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake:** Writing a one-line prompt like *"write a post about my cafe."*
  **Fix:** Add a role, an audience, and a format. *"You are a friendly marketer writing for local regulars. Write a 60-word Instagram caption about our new oat-milk latte. End with a question."*

- **Mistake:** Starting a brand-new chat every time the answer disappoints you.
  **Fix:** Stay in the same chat and send one specific follow-up. The AI keeps the context, so iteration is faster than restarting.

- **Mistake:** Asking the AI to *"make it better"* without saying how.
  **Fix:** Name the change — tone, length, audience, or structure. *"More playful, cut to 80 words, target first-time customers"* is three times more useful than *"better."*

- **Mistake:** Letting the AI invent facts you didn't give it.
  **Fix:** Paste the source material (the job ad, the meeting notes, the article) so the AI summarizes what you provided instead of guessing.

## What this means for you

- **If you use AI for everyday tasks:** Try the role + audience + format pattern the next time you draft a text message, plan a meal, or summarize a long article. You'll get a useful answer on the first try instead of the third.

- **If you use AI for work:** Save your best prompts in a notes app. A good prompt for writing job ads, client emails, or weekly reports can be reused dozens of times with small tweaks. Within a week, you'll write prompts faster than you type regular emails.

- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one weekly task — a meeting recap, a weekly menu, a study summary — and write a detailed prompt for it using the five steps. Use it three times, tweak it once, and you have the whole skill.
